story_text.value:
rbit is a self hosted git forge designed around three core philosophies: speed, security, and efficiency.

We built rbit using Rust, Axum, Askama, Gitoxide, SQLite + redb, HTMX + Tailwind. Every piece of the stack was carefully considered to provide users with the fastest possible experience working with their repos without sacrificing the functionality you've come to expect from your existing git forge.

Our team is actively working to help make rbit the best it can be and we'd love to get your feedback while we continue improving!

rbit is built using rbit and it's CI/CD pipeline, we are dogfooding as we build it in the open. It has been localized into 9 languages including: English, Spanish, Portuguese, French, German, Russian, Chinese (Simplified), Japanese, and Korean. If you're a native speaker we would happily accept translation fixes!

story_text.value:
My mom is a photographer and an artist. This year, she complained that she doesn't quite enjoy the existing options for storing, sharing, and organizing her work.

After a few sessions, I think we got into the ballpark of what it should look like if we weren't Google or SmugMug: with a host of extra features (clutter detection, decent search, book and album writing, even calorie and activity tracking, and a few other conveniences)

The original intention was to build an application that would serve our family. But I feel like it's growing into something bigger as people are joining in. If you want to try, here's an invite code (capped at 50 signups): YRASHK-7ZXA-S3K3-DM8V

story_text.value:
I've long thought about how we're influenced by CPU architectures, and importantly, their ISAs.

In a discussion at a meetup, I brought up a topic that interested me for a while: how would an ISA that exposes memory and cache interactions in a more explicit way (because if you think about it, memory is very much I/O), as opposed to being smart and predictive on its own?

An obscure interest, of course. Nevertheless, I wanted to build a quick prototype after that.

What ended up transpiring was a bit larger. A multicore architecture with tiered stores, capabilities, a JIT'd emulator, Verilog RTL with a simulator, a small microkernel OS, UI, JIT Forth, an assembler in its own assembly, a bootstrapping C99 compiler, a few games, a visual debugger, and a few other things.

(This also shows just how far a directed LLM process can go in little time)

title.value: Show HN: Strata Architecture

story_text.value:
I've seen too many slow-log queries with a GROUP BY that makes Postgres blow up, so for the last two weeks or so I've been working on Straum. You declare the aggregates as a view, and Straum answers over HTTP (other transports might be added). I've been using the New York taxi dataset as a benchmark. On the heavier GROUP BYs I see about 1,000x to 5,000x. It's written in Rust (of course).

It leans on Postgres replication slots, logical or physical, to get its data. Postgres stays the source of truth.

What do you think?

Benchmark: https://janbjorge.github.io/straum/benchmark.html Repo: https://github.com/janbjorge/straum

title.value: Show HN: Straum – PostgreSQL Group by in Microseconds

story_text.value:
Hi HN. This all started when I was targeted by one of those fake video call schemes we hear so much about lately. I was invited into a video call with someone posing as a person I’d met at a conference, and I was close to being fooled before their “audio problems” became increasingly suspicious. When Tavus announced its Griffin-Lite model last month, they claimed 48% of callers mistook it for a human. I think to avoid future scenarios like my own, it’s clear we need irrefutable proof of who’s on the other side of your call and not simply a judgement call.

So I’ve been working these last few months on a solution that proves the person on the other side of a call is using a genuine camera and is who they say they are, without sacrificing privacy and avoiding the pitfalls of using detection.

The result is Apertrue Witness. You can find details on how it works in the first comment, on the landing page, and full technical detail here (https://witness.apertrue.photo/how).

Witness is live today on macOS 27+ and iPhone (https://witness.apertrue.photo/download, Windows and Android coming soon). You can check out a previously verified call here: https://witness.apertrue.photo/verify/sample and the verifier here: https://github.com/Apertrue/witness-verify. It’s free while we complete our independent audit.

title.value: Show HN: Apertrue Witness – proof of camera and identity for video calls

story_text.value: The world of AI used to have people training models for solving substantial issues - like beat world's best go players or solving protein folding. Now that the AI got good, perhaps we forgot a bit how to do it. There is still cheap hardware around for tinkerers and people who want to continue good AI legacy. But the hardware may miss software. It is for those people that I started working on zyx long time ago - ML library in hopes of running on any hardware. One example of such hardware is tenstorrent. But the basics must be built first. And so today I'm showing you skamandros. A tiny, self-contained driver and compiler for tenstorrent cards (tested on p100a). PTX like input, mostly abstracted away hardware details (other than tiling), automatic optimizations and operation fusion. Hope you can use this software to write AI models that people can like.

title.value: Show HN: 1MB Tenstorrent driver with ptx like kernels

story_text.value:
Hello HN,

I built `atl`, a Rust CLI for Jira, Confluence, Bitbucket, Jira Service Management, Trello and Atlassian Admin. The same commands work on Cloud and Data Center (on-prem).

It's built for both people and AI agents: an --agent mode that outputs JSON and never prompts, a built-in MCP server with 136 tools, and a read-only login so an agent can't change anything. Confluence pages can be edited as Markdown and kept in git.

It has SDK support as well for Python, TypeScript/JS, and WASM.

Any feedback and contributions are welcome!

story_text.value:
Hi HN, we’re building Widefleet for teams building internal apps and workflows with coding agents.

Think Vercel or Cloudflare, with company login (SSO), app sharing, and controls for IT to manage who can access each app and which company systems it can connect to. Apps run as separate workers with per-app databases and object storage. You can also fully customize and manage connectors to internal systems, so your other users don’t have to handle API keys etc. themselves. Cron jobs and queues support background tasks and recurring workflows.

There’s now a hosted version, so give it a try and let us know what you think!

Try it: https://app.widefleet.com Code: https://github.com/widefleet/widefleet

Curious how you’re dealing with vibe-coded apps at work, whether you built them yourself or ended up maintaining someone else’s.

story_text.value:
Hi HN!

Here to show off a project that took 18 months, 7KLOC, and more importantly, 194 kilometres of walking! In a nutshell, I wanted to make the famous silhouette animation “Bad Apple” with Strava, which is an exercise tracking app that visualizes where you walk/run on a map. To use the earth as my canvas, I had to do a lot of coding in the prep work to plan where I would walk for each frame of the animation. As I explain in the video, my problem solving/coding steps were something like this:

- split video into frames, determine a good framerate

- detect contours with OpenCV for each frame. Since frames are very diverse, I had to start with some heuristics for choosing contours and ultimately make a GUI to manually curate all 438 of them (e.g. some frames had many small contours while others had a few important ones, and the video is constantly inverting colours). Output of this work was an intermediate json list of x,y coordinates representing the path along contours

- convert these cartesian coordinates into the Universal Transverse Mercator coordinate system, which represents the earth in a cartesian system (as opposed to GPS which doesn’t lend to adding relative distances in degrees very well)

- convert UTM to GPS using a package, then to the GPX file format which is universally accepted

- Import GPX files into an app that shows where I am and where I need to walk (I used Gaia GPS). Then I turned on Strava in the background and walked for ~18 months until this was done.

I also had to make a bunch of custom software to visualize these walks and make montages of them, like a script to pull polylines from the Strava API, a custom polyline renderer, a script to censor my strava activities a bit, and much more. I’m so proud of this work, it feels like it stands out in a sea of code-only bad apple projects that have become easier to automate with AI, and I hope it can go down as one of the greats in the bad apple colossus of work!

Video: https://youtu.be/HxdQawDIlnU GitHub: https://github.com/kevinlinxc/badapple-strava

Happy to answer any questions!

title.value: Show HN: Bad Apple but it's Strava [video]
